source.title_on_document: Cultivating design creativity of vocational students: A model of project-based learning in AI-enabled immersive virtual environments

paper_design_summary: Two intact first-year classes of an Interior Art Design major at a vocational college in Fuzhou, China, were reportedly randomly assigned to conditions, one class per arm, during a 12-week Public Space Interior Design course with the same instructor (p. 12). One class used project-based learning in an AI-enabled immersive virtual environment (PICO 4 VR headsets, SketchUp, and an AI teaching assistant built on the iFLYTEK Xinghuo large model); the other used traditional project-based learning with drawing tablets and AutoCAD (pp. 13-14). The analyzed outcomes are self-report Likert questionnaires on design creativity (pretest and posttest), learning engagement, and learning experience; the classroom workflow included a design/presentation rubric and self-, peer-, and teacher evaluations, but no reported research outcome was scored on student products (p. 11, Refinement; pp. 15-17, surveys and Data collection and analysis; pp. 23-24, Limitations and future research).

studies.label: Two-class quasi-experiment (Public Space Interior Design course)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Two intact classes, chosen to be similar on entrance scores and prior design experience, were randomly assigned to conditions, one class per arm. Individual students were not randomized. The paper calls the design quasi-experimental (p. 12).
assignment.quote: The two selected classes were then randomly assigned to a control group (33 students) and an experimental group (31 students) to reduce the likelihood of systematic baseline differences between the groups.
assignment.locator: p. 12, Research design, Participants; design called quasi-experimental at p. 12, Experimental design

arms.name: AI-IVE-PBL
arms.description: Project-based learning in the AI-enabled immersive virtual environment: PICO 4 VR devices, SketchUp, and an AI teaching assistant on the Xinghuo large model

arms.name: T-PBL
arms.description: Traditional project-based learning with electronic drawing tablets, AutoCAD, images and videos, and teacher-led case explanation and group discussion

participants.exclusions: 64 questionnaires collected (33 control, 31 experimental); 63 valid retained after excluding invalid responses (p. 17). Table 1 gives 31 AI-IVE-PBL and 32 T-PBL, so the excluded response came from the control class. The 64 count is the students in the two randomized classes; randomization was at the class level.
participants.who: First-year Interior Art Design students at Fuzhou Software Technology Vocational College; 29 male, 34 female; 96.83 percent aged 19 to 20
participants.quote: The sample consisted of 63 participants, comprising 29 males and 34 females (see Table 1).
participants.locator: p. 18, Analysis of students' situation and Table 1; p. 17, Data collection and analysis

ai_tool.name_model: AI teaching assistant integrating the API of the Xinghuo cognitive large model (iFLYTEK), inside the AI-IVE platform of the National Engineering Research Center for E-learning, Central China Normal University
ai_tool.how_used: Embodied digital-human assistant that answers student questions orally, suggests materials, uses layered questioning, generates knowledge maps, and gives feedback and optimization suggestions on 3D design simulations (pp. 13-14). It is bundled with VR immersion, so the contrast is not AI alone.

task.description: Interior design course projects: Aviation Exhibition Hall Design, Memorial Hall Design, and Construction Drawing Deepening Design (p. 9)

outcomes.name: Creative ability (design creativity survey subscale)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Four self-report items on a 5-point Likert scale adapted from Runco et al. (2001), e.g. 'I generate design ideas for interior spaces and bring them to fruition' (p. 15, Appendix 1). Posttest compared by ANCOVA with the design creativity pretest as covariate. The paper states it relies exclusively on self-report questionnaires (p. 23).

outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Four self-report items on a 5-point Likert scale adapted from Runco et al. (2001), e.g. 'I excel at proposing novel ideas to solve problems' (p. 15, Appendix 1). ANCOVA with pretest covariate.

eligibility.reason: Criterion 3 is not met: the analyzed creativity outcomes are self-report questionnaires, and no reported research outcome was scored on student products (p. 15, Design creativity survey; p. 19, Table 2; pp. 23-24, Limitations and future research). Classroom design and presentation evaluations are described but are not reported as study outcome data (p. 11, Refinement). Criterion 1 is met by the reported random assignment of two intact classes during ordinary coursework (p. 12, Participants and Experimental design), with one class per arm; the authors nevertheless call the design quasi-experimental. The intervention bundles VR and the LLM assistant, so it does not isolate the LLM contribution (pp. 13-14, Experimental design and Experimental environment). Criterion 2 is met with 63 students analyzed (31 AI-IVE-PBL and 32 T-PBL; pp. 18-19, Tables 1-2). The self-report-only study remains excluded from the core dataset and context evidence.

one_line_finding: Against traditional project-based learning, the VR-plus-LLM-assistant class reported higher self-rated creative ability (4.00 vs 3.73, F = 7.465, p = .008) and design ability (3.98 vs 3.62, F = 9.630, p = .003) but not innovative thinking (4.05 vs 3.85, p = .114), on self-report scales only (p. 19, Table 2).
